## Tutorial 2 Exercises markdown

# Exercise 2.3

First import the relevant data and create the dataframe

```{r}
library(glmnet)
library(effects)
set.seed(333)

data <- read.csv("utrechthousinglarge.csv")

# i'll also make buildyear into age to keeep it aligned with the exercise
data$age <- as.numeric(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")) - data$buildyear

# choose balcony as factor as well, like bathroom but one more option
data$balcony <- as.factor(data$balcony)
data$bathrooms <- as.factor(data$bathrooms)
# also monument and energy efficient for the same reason
data$monument <- as.factor(data$monument)
data$energy.eff <- as.factor(data$energy.eff)

# make final dataset without the buildyear (replaced by age) and excluding taxvalue
data2 <- subset(data, select = -c(buildyear, taxvalue))

```

We did the preprocessing, now we want to use a formula to set up a regression model on all other variables. 

```{r}
# Create matrix with interactions and polynomials
ff <- retailvalue ~ .^2 + I(age^2)
X <- model.matrix(ff, data2)[, -1]
y <- data2$retailvalue

```

Now set up the training and testing splits and look at how different penalised regressions predict house prices.

```{r}
# do the split
train <- sample(1:nrow(X), nrow(X) / 2)
test <- (-train)

# first, lasso 
lasso <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1)
lassopred <- predict(lasso, s = "lambda.min", newx = X[test, ])
lassomse <- mean((lassopred - y[test])^2)

# now ridge
ridge <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 0)
ridgepred <- predict(ridge, s = "lambda.min", newx = X[test, ])
ridgemse <- mean((ridgepred - y[test])^2)

# and adaptive lasso
# use the lasso coefficients as an initial estimate
initial <- as.numeric(coef(lasso, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
w <- 1 / abs(initial)
alasso <- cv.glmnet(X[train, ], y[train], alpha = 1, penalty.factor = w)
alassopred <- predict(alasso, s = "lambda.min", newx = X[test, ])
alassomse <- mean((ridgepred - y[test])^2)

plot(lasso, type = "l")
plot(ridge, type = "l")
plot(alasso, type = "l")

lsel <- sum(coef(lasso, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0)
rsel <- sum(coef(ridge, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0)
alsel <- sum(coef(alasso, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0)

res <- data.frame(RMSE = c(lassomse, ridgemse, alassomse), Selected = c(lsel, rsel, alsel))
print(res)

```
We can now do the simulation part of the exercise.

```{r}
# 1. Create simulated dataframe fixing all variables except 'age'
sim_data <- data2[rep(1, 100), ] 
sim_data$age <- seq(min(data2$age), max(data2$age), length.out = 100)
sim_data$retailvalue <- 0 # Placeholder

# 2. Append to original data, create matrix, and isolate simulated rows
combined_data <- rbind(data2, sim_data)
X_combined <- model.matrix(ff, combined_data)[, -1]
X_sim <- X_combined[(nrow(data2) + 1):nrow(X_combined), ]

# 3. Predict outcomes to plot the marginal effect
sim_predictions <- predict(lasso, s = "lambda.min", newx = X_sim)
plot(sim_data$age, sim_predictions, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Predicted Retail Value")

```
Claudes answer to the effects question:

```{r}
best_model <- lasso
pred_vars  <- setdiff(names(data2), "retailvalue")

effect_curve <- function(var, ngrid = 20) {
  col <- data2[[var]]
  base <- data2[1, , drop = FALSE]
  # fix all other variables at median (numeric) or most common level (factor)
  for (v in pred_vars) {
    if (is.factor(data2[[v]])) {
      base[[v]] <- factor(names(which.max(table(data2[[v]]))), levels = levels(data2[[v]]))
    } else base[[v]] <- median(data2[[v]])
  }
  if (is.factor(col)) {
    vals <- levels(col)
    new  <- base[rep(1, length(vals)), ]
    new[[var]] <- factor(vals, levels = levels(col))
  } else {
    vals <- seq(quantile(col, 0.05), quantile(col, 0.95), length.out = ngrid)
    new  <- base[rep(1, ngrid), ]
    new[[var]] <- vals
  }
  # Stack new rows under the original data so dummies/columns match, then drop originals
  combined <- rbind(data2, new)
  Xall <- model.matrix(ff, combined)[, -1]
  Xnew <- Xall[(nrow(data2) + 1):nrow(combined), , drop = FALSE]
  list(x = vals, pred = as.numeric(predict(best_model, Xnew, s = "lambda.min")))
}
 
curves <- lapply(pred_vars, effect_curve); names(curves) <- pred_vars

# Plot each effect
par(mar = c(1,1,1,1))
for (v in pred_vars) {
  cu <- curves[[v]]
  if (is.character(cu$x)) barplot(cu$pred, names.arg = cu$x, main = v, ylab = "predicted value")
  else plot(cu$x, cu$pred, type = "l", main = v, xlab = v, ylab = "predicted value")
}
 
# Importance = range of predicted price when varying that variable only
importance <- sort(sapply(curves, function(cu) diff(range(cu$pred))), decreasing = TRUE)
print(importance)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1)); barplot(rev(importance), horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
                              main = "Effect range by original variable")
 
```


# Exercise 2.4

Time for the monte carlo simulation to see how often they pick the relevant variables.

First need to implement all the processes for the simulation.

```{r}
# define parameters
n     <- 50     
p     <- 10       
R     <- 1000  
sigma <- 1       

# then the coefficients
# use rep() to set the remaining beta coefs to 1 value
beta       <- c(2, -1, 1, -1, 1, rep(0, p - 5))
relevant   <- which(beta != 0)    
irrelevant <- which(beta == 0)    

# make a matrix that tracks the 2 types of mistakes each regression makes
irrelsel <- matrix(NA, nrow = R, ncol = 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("lasso", "ridge", "enet", "adaptive")))
relnsel <- matrix(NA, nrow = R, ncol = 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("lasso", "ridge" , "enet", "adaptive")))

# now for the simulation loop
for (r in 1:R) {
  # initialise the normal distribution we need for eps and x
  # separately to make them different, and x needs to be a matrix to work
  z   <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  x   <- 1 * z 
  eps <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)
  
  # use %*% for matrix multiplication
  y   <- x %*% beta + eps
  
  # now start with the regressions
  # first lasso
  lassocv <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)
  lassob  <- as.numeric(coef(lassocv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  
  # elastic net 
  encv <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0.5)
  enb  <- as.numeric(coef(encv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  
  # ridge for fun
  ridgecv <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0)
  ridgeb <- as.numeric(coef(ridgecv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]

  # adaptive lasso using ridge coefficients as initial estimators
  w        <- 1 / abs(ridgeb)                                   
  alcv  <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, penalty.factor = w)
  alb   <- as.numeric(coef(alcv, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  
  # look at which vars were selected
  sel <- cbind(lassob != 0, enb != 0, ridgeb != 0, alb != 0) 
  
  irrelsel[r, ] <- colSums(sel[irrelevant, ])      # irrelevant variables that were selected
  relnsel[r, ] <- colSums(!sel[relevant, ])
  
}
  
```

See what this results in:

```{r}
results <- rbind("avg false positives (out of p-5)" = colMeans(irrelsel),
                 "avg false negatives (out of 5)"   = colMeans(relnsel)
                 )
print(round(results, 3))
```


# Exercise 2.5

```{r}
library(lars); library(glmnet)
fit_lar   <- lars(x, y, type = "lar")
fit_lasso <- lars(x, y, type = "lasso")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot(fit_lar); plot(fit_lasso)   # compare the paths
cv <- cv.lars(x, y, K = 10, type = "lasso")             # CV over the fraction s
coef(fit_lasso, s = cv$index[which.min(cv$cv)], mode = "fraction")
fit_cd <- glmnet(x, y)                                  # coordinate descent for comparison
```

## Tutorial 3

# Exercise 3.2

For this exercise we look at the data for credit modelling.
Our main focus is to model the probability of a credit default using penalised regression. 

As categorical variables, I choose (based on website):
- CAT_GAMBLING: Gambling category (none, low, high)
- CAT_DEBT: 1 if the customer has debt; 0 otherwise
- CAT_CREDIT_CARD: 1 if the customer has a credit card; 0 otherwise
- CAT_MORTGAGE: 1 if the customer has a mortgage; 0 otherwise
I exclude CAT_SAVINGS_ACCOUNT and CAT_DEPENDENTS as I dont find them relevant enough (arbitrary)

Want to investigate how different penalised regressions perform in predicting probability of default and to understand which factors are important to determine that probability. 

```{r}
datacredit <- read.csv("credit_score.csv")

# set the categoirical terms we chose
datacredit$CAT_GAMBLING <- as.factor(datacredit$CAT_GAMBLING)
datacredit$CAT_DEBT <- as.factor(datacredit$CAT_DEBT)
datacredit$CAT_CREDIT_CARD <- as.factor(datacredit$CAT_CREDIT_CARD)
datacredit$CAT_MORTGAGE <- as.factor(datacredit$CAT_MORTGAGE)

# now get rid of unneeded data columns
datacredit$CUST_ID <- NULL

# define the X and y, want to test for default
X <- model.matrix(DEFAULT ~ ., data = datacredit)[, -1]
y <- datacredit$DEFAULT

# set the training and testing samples
traintest <- sample(1:nrow(X), size = 0.8 * nrow(X))
xtrain <- X[traintest, ]
ytrain <- y[traintest]
xtest <- X[-traintest, ]
ytest <- y[-traintest]

# Scale features
xscale <- scale(X)
xtrainscale <- scale(xtrain)
xtestscale <- scale(xtest, 
                       center = attr(xtrainscale, "scaled:center"), 
                       scale = attr(xtrainscale, "scaled:scale"))

```

We have the data ready now, so we can look at how the regressions perform. For the cross validation I'll use k-fold, since the data isn't a time series.
I'll try to include as many as possible.

```{r}
# first basic lasso
# apparently should inlude "binomial" since default is a binary outcome
lassocv <- cv.glmnet(xtrainscale, ytrain, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, nfolds = 5)

# can then predict using this cross validated lasso
# Predict classes ("class") using the optimal lambda strictly minimizing CV error
y_pred <- predict(lassocv, s = "lambda.min", newx = xtestscale, type = "class")
test_accuracy <- mean(as.numeric(y_pred) == ytest)

print(paste("Optimal lambda:", round(lassocv$lambda.min, 4)))
print(paste("Out-of-Sample Test Accuracy:", round(test_accuracy, 4)))


# Get important features
# Extract coefficients and remove the intercept
coefsl <- as.matrix(coef(lassocv))[-1, , drop = FALSE]

# Filter non-zero coefficients and sort by absolute value
important_features <- coefsl[coefsl[, 1] != 0, , drop = FALSE]
important_features <- important_features[order(abs(important_features[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE), , drop = FALSE]

print("Top 10 features selected by Lasso Logistic Regression:")
print(head(important_features, 10))
```
